prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, reaching systematic uncertainties at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B015, Katori and Ye, as a single-part prize. Nothing in the first-round exchange weakened the scientific core, which five members state in the same terms. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is the original idea, because it makes the light shift cancel for a large ensemble of neutral atoms at once. Ye's group demonstrated the accuracy and the many-body-limited operation that made it a practical instrument at about 1e-18, and independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL) have reproduced the performance with agreed comparisons. The chair asks what wording would separate this from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. I would tie the citation to the invention of the lattice scheme and its realization at the 1e-18 level, and not to frequency measurement or atom control in general. That wording says what is new: a neutral-atom ensemble measured with very low statistical noise while the systematic shifts are controlled. It also fits what the five B015 citations already share. As a theorist of stochastic systems I read the case through the error budget, and this is the case where the budget is documented and cross-checked rather than asserted.
statement.case_against: The honest weak points are three. First, a committee may judge a measurement capability to be a lesser kind of achievement than a new phenomenon, and may see it as incremental after 2005 and 2012. I think the lattice clock is a distinct concept with distinct physics, but this is a judgment and not a proof. Second, the two-name credit leaves out Ludlow, Lemke, Lemonde, Le Targat and the single-ion clock groups, who reached comparable uncertainties by other routes. Third, the SI redefinition of the second is pending. I still regard these as questions of framing and boundary, not as evidence against the science. My own earlier first choice, B023 (KPZ), remains attractive to me but has one preference and an unclean credit list, since the exact-solution authors are outside the supplied names, so I keep it only as an alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B006 because a concrete prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald flat bands) was followed by an unexpected experimental result, and he asks what evidence would move members toward or away from B015.
responses.response: I accept that prediction followed by surprise is the most compelling pattern of discovery, and I think B006 has it. But the same maturity caveat that Danielsson states himself decides it for me this year. The pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated states are still debated, and the results depend on twist-angle disorder, so a citation would have to be written around observation and could be overtaken. I would answer his question in this way. Evidence that the superconductivity has an agreed mechanism, or that the correlated phases are reproduced across devices with controlled disorder, would move me strongly toward B006. For that reason I support B006 as the leading candidate for a later year, and I would not make a second part of this year's prize out of it.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether B015 needs a principled reason to omit B006, whether a two-part prize should be explored, and whether the SI redefinition of the second should be a precondition.
responses.response: My principled line is the one I gave to Danielsson: maturity of interpretation, not importance. B006 may well be the larger wave, but its central scientific question is open, whereas B015 is settled and independently confirmed. I do not favour a two-part prize this year. A second part would be chosen to complete a configuration, and no pairing has broad support, since every member's preferred configuration is a single part. On the SI redefinition I repeat my round-1 view and sharpen it. It is a supporting consideration, because the demonstrated performance, the comparisons between laboratories and the tests of gravitational redshift already carry the physics. The committee should not tie a scientific judgment to a metrological-body timetable.

responses.point: Lindroth, whose field is precision atomic spectroscopy, ranks B015 first on atomic-structure grounds (magic wavelengths, blackbody shifts), but treats the boundary with single-ion optical clocks and incremental-in-kind novelty as open questions.
responses.response: I rely on her expertise for the atomic-structure judgment, and I take her incremental-in-kind concern seriously, because it is the central objection. My answer is that the lattice clock was not a refinement of the ion clock. It changed the statistics, by interrogating very many atoms at once, and it required the magic-wavelength concept to make that possible. That is a different route to the same accuracy, with a different error budget. It does not rest on the 2012 trapping and control techniques. This is the principled line between inventor and refiner that the chair asks for. Katori supplied the concept and Ye's group demonstrated that it holds at 1e-18. Groups that reached comparable levels later, or by other physical routes, are important, but they do not alter who did what first. I would still welcome her view on whether the citation should name the lattice scheme explicitly.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B055 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) for the new organizing principle of band topology, and himself identifies credit as its weak point, since Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy fall outside the supplied names. He now treats B015 as his second alternative.
responses.response: I agree that B055 is a mature and conceptually important case, and that its confirmation is broad. The credit gap he describes is the difference between the two cases for me. For B015 the supplied names match the invention and the realization, and the people left out are refiners or parallel routes. For B055 the people left out proposed the HgTe structure and the three-dimensional generalization, so a three-name prize would divide work that is hard to divide. I would not exclude B055, and a cleaner framing might change my view. As framed on this shortlist, the attribution problem is larger than in B015, and I would hold it as a candidate for a later year with a deliberately chosen framing.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that optical lattice clocks are a distinct step from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and not a refinement of recognized work.
Whether the omission of Ludlow, Lemke, Lemonde, Le Targat and the single-ion clock groups will be seen as an acceptable boundary for a two-name credit.
Whether the SI redefinition of the second will be treated as a precondition by colleagues despite my view that it is a supporting factor only.

I rely on recollection of the clock literature and have not verified specific uncertainty records or priority claims, and my judgment of the atomic-structure details is made from outside the subfield.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My documented work (inertial particles in turbulence, random matrices, stochastic dynamics, neural networks) and listed co-authors do not include Katori, Ye or any other shortlisted name. My statistical-physics background is relevant only to B023, which I hold as an alternative and not as the preferred prize. Nothing in round 1 changes this disclosure.
